A '''parabolic partial differential equation''' is a type of [[partial differential equation]] (PDE). Parabolic PDEs are used to describe a wide variety of time-dependent phenomena in, for example, [[engineering science]], [[quantum mechanics]] and [[financial mathematics]]. Examples include the [[heat equation]], [[Schrödinger_equation#Time-dependent_equation|time-dependent Schrödinger equation]] and the [[Black–Scholes equation]].

== Definition ==
To define the simplest kind of parabolic PDE, consider a real-valued function <math>u(x, y)</math> of two independent real variables, <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>. A [[Partial differential equation#Classification|second-order, linear, constant-coefficient PDE]] for <math>u</math> takes the form

:<math>Au_{xx} + 2Bu_{xy} + Cu_{yy} + Du_x + Eu_y + F = 0,</math>

where the subscripts denote the first- and second-order [[partial derivative]]s with respect to <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>. The PDE is classified as ''parabolic'' if the coefficients of the principal part (i.e. the terms containing the second derivatives of <math>u</math>) satisfy the condition{{sfn | Zauderer | 2006 | p=124}}

:<math>B^2 - AC = 0.</math>

Usually <math>x</math> represents one-dimensional position and <math>y</math> represents time, and the PDE is solved subject to prescribed [[initial condition|initial]] and [[boundary condition]]s. Equations with <math>B^2 - AC < 0</math> are termed [[Elliptic partial differential equation|elliptic]] while those with <math>B^2 - AC > 0</math> are [[Hyperbolic partial differential equation|hyperbolic]]. The name "parabolic" is used because the assumption on the coefficients is the same as the condition for the analytic geometry equation <math>A x^2 + 2B xy + C y^2 + D x + E y + F = 0</math> to define a planar [[Parabola#General case|parabola]].

The basic example of a parabolic PDE is the one-dimensional [[heat equation]]

:<math>u_t = \alpha\,u_{xx},</math>

where <math>u(x,t)</math> is the temperature at position <math>x</math> along a thin rod at time <math>t</math> and <math>\alpha</math> is a positive constant called the [[thermal diffusivity]].

The heat equation says, roughly, that temperature at a given time and point rises or falls at a rate proportional to the difference between the temperature at that point and the average temperature near that point. The quantity <math>u_{xx}</math> measures how far off the temperature is from satisfying the mean value property of [[harmonic functions]].

The concept of a parabolic PDE can be generalized in several ways.
For instance, the flow of heat through a material body is governed by the three-dimensional heat equation

:<math>u_t = \alpha\,\Delta u,</math>

where

:<math>\Delta u := \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}+\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}+\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial z^2},</math>

denotes the [[Laplace operator]] acting on <math>u</math>.  This equation is the prototype of a ''multi-dimensional parabolic'' PDE.{{sfn | Zauderer | 2006 | p=139}}

Noting that <math>-\Delta</math> is an [[elliptic operator]] suggests a broader definition of a parabolic PDE:

:<math>u_t = -Lu,</math>

where <math>L</math> is a second-order [[elliptic operator]]
(implying that <math>L</math> must be [[Positive operator|positive]];
a case where <math>u_t = +Lu</math> is considered below).

A system of partial differential equations for a vector <math>u</math> can also be parabolic.
For example, such a system is hidden in an equation of the form

:<math>\nabla \cdot (a(x) \nabla u(x)) + b(x)^\text{T} \nabla u(x) + cu(x) = f(x)</math>

if the matrix-valued function <math>a(x)</math> has a [[Kernel (algebra)|kernel]] of dimension 1.

== Solution ==
Under broad assumptions, an initial/boundary-value problem for a linear parabolic PDE has a solution for all time. The solution <math>u(x,t)</math>, as a function of <math>x</math> for a fixed time <math>t > 0</math>, is generally smoother than the initial data <math>u(x,0) = u_0(x)</math>, according to [[Regularity theory#Parabolic and Hyperbolic regularity theory|parabolic regularity theory]].

For a nonlinear parabolic PDE, a solution of an initial/boundary-value problem might explode in a [[Mathematical singularity|singularity]] within a finite amount of time. It can be difficult to determine whether a solution exists for all time, or to understand the singularities that do arise. Such interesting questions arise in the [[Poincaré conjecture#Solution|solution of the Poincaré conjecture]] via [[Ricci flow]].{{citation needed|date=July 2020}}

== Backward parabolic equation ==
One occasionally encounters a so-called ''backward parabolic PDE'', which takes the form <math>u_t = Lu</math> (note the absence of a minus sign).

An initial-value problem for the backward heat equation,

:<math>\begin{cases} u_{t} = -\Delta u & \textrm{on} \ \ \Omega \times (0,T), \\ u=0 & \textrm{on} \ \ \partial\Omega \times (0,T), \\ u = f & \textrm{on} \ \ \Omega \times \left \{ 0 \right \}. \end{cases}</math>

is equivalent to a final-value problem for the ordinary heat equation,

:<math>\begin{cases} u_{t} = \Delta u & \textrm{on} \ \ \Omega \times (0,T), \\ u=0
& \textrm{on} \ \ \partial\Omega \times (0,T), \\ u = f & \textrm{on} \ \ \Omega \times \left \{ T \right \}. \end{cases} </math>

Similarly to a final-value problem for a parabolic PDE, an initial-value problem for a backward parabolic PDE is usually not [[well-posed]] (solutions often grow unbounded in finite time, or even fail to exist). Nonetheless, these problems are important for the study of the reflection of singularities of solutions to various other PDEs.{{sfn | Taylor | 1975 }}
